business_patterns.top_pattern: GA and PA authorization and facility mapping issues need validation before action
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: PPO Local inpatient authorization flags and facility mapping in GA and PA
key_driver_codes: Hip and Femur Procedures Except Major Joint with CC
Kidney and Urinary Tract Infections without MCC
Septicemia or Severe Sepsis without Mechanical Ventilation >96 Hours without MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: The largest issue is not a clear utilization or reimbursement trend but a validation problem. In GA, a major share of the increase sits in authorization code redistribution, and both GA and PA also show additional spend in a Not Mapped facility bucket for authorized inpatient claims. These signals should be treated as data and classification issues first, because business action on utilization management or provider economics could be misdirected until the mapping is confirmed.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: If authorization and facility mapping are wrong, policy, network, and UM actions will target the wrong problem.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Run a joint UM, reimbursement, and data-quality audit of authorization-to-claim mapping and facility crosswalks in GA and PA for the listed inpatient DRGs before changing policy, provider strategy, or denial rules.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The increase is explicitly flagged as an authorization or mapping shift and includes unmapped facility values, so the data must be validated before business action.
evidence_summary: GA authorization code redistribution accounts for about $1.8M, concentrated in hip/femur, UTI, metabolic disorder, and sepsis admissions.
GA PPO Local claims in the Not Mapped facility bucket add about $213K, led by about $89K in metabolic disorders and about $80K in hip/femur cases.
PA PPO Local claims in the Not Mapped facility bucket add about $113K, including about $79K at ATLANTICARE REGIONAL MEDICAL CTR and about $34K in sepsis cases.

business_patterns.top_pattern: GA authorized acute hospital admissions are up, with added cost pressure at DCH
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: GA PPO Local acute hospital inpatient admissions with required authorization
key_driver_codes: Kidney and Urinary Tract Infections without MCC
Hip and Femur Procedures Except Major Joint with CC
Septicemia or Severe Sepsis without Mechanical Ventilation >96 Hours without MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: GA acute hospital spend is rising because authorized admissions increased and some cases also cost more per stay. The increase is concentrated at DCH REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER and in a small set of inpatient DRGs, especially UTI, cellulitis, hip/femur, and sepsis. This is a direct UM and provider-performance issue rather than a broad statewide pricing change.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: This is one of the clearest actionable inpatient cost drivers because both admission growth and payment intensity are contributing.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Launch a joint UM and network review for GA PPO Local acute hospital admissions, starting with DCH REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER and the listed DRGs, to test admission appropriateness, length-of-stay drivers, and reimbursement terms together.
evidence_summary: DCH REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER drives about $193K, with 12 more admissions and about $16K higher paid per admit.
UTI and cellulitis admissions add about $185K and $176K, each with roughly 24 more admissions.
Hip/femur and sepsis add about $325K more, with 14 to 17 additional admissions in GA acute hospitals.

business_patterns.top_pattern: GA inpatient growth is concentrated in infection, sepsis, cellulitis, and femur fracture cases
key_driver_codes: DSPL IT FX LT FEMUR INITIAL CLOS FX
Hip and Femur Procedures Except Major Joint with CC
Kidney and Urinary Tract Infections without MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: GA clinical pressure is not broad-based. It is concentrated in a small set of infection, sepsis, cellulitis, and femur fracture presentations that are driving inpatient use and, in some cases, higher paid per admit. This clinical concentration helps explain why GA authorized acute hospital costs are rising and gives UM and clinical teams a focused set of pathways to review.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Targeted clinical management is more likely to reduce avoidable inpatient use here than broad policy changes.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Have clinical and UM teams review admission appropriateness, observation versus inpatient use, and discharge planning for GA UTI, sepsis, cellulitis, and femur fracture episodes.
evidence_summary: UTI site not specified adds about $245K with 30 more admissions in kidney and urinary infection stays.
Sepsis unspecified organism adds about $196K with 21 more admissions.
Cellulitis of the left lower limb adds about $119K with 12 more admissions and about $2.7K higher paid per admit.
Left femur fracture adds about $198K with 15 more admissions.

business_patterns.pattern_details: Outside GA, the recurring operational theme is straightforward admission growth in authorized acute hospital cases, not broad reimbursement inflation. CA and the CT / MO / NY / PA cluster both show higher inpatient volume in a short list of DRGs, including hip/femur, UTI, metabolic disorders, and sepsis. This points to utilization management and provider engagement as the main levers.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: When the increase is mainly volume-led, tightening admission management is likely to be more effective than contract action alone.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Prioritize pre-admit and post-admit review for the listed DRGs in CA and CT / MO / NY / PA, with targeted outreach to SSM HEALTH DEPAUL HOSPITAL - ST. LOUIS in MO.
evidence_summary: In CA, hip/femur admissions add about $173K with 10 more admissions, even as paid per admit declined slightly.
In CA, UTI admissions add about $127K with 13 more admissions.
In CT / MO / NY / PA, SSM HEALTH DEPAUL HOSPITAL - ST. LOUIS adds about $76K with 6 more admissions.
NY hip/femur and metabolic disorder clusters add about $195K combined, with 6 more admissions in each cluster.

business_patterns.pattern_details: OH shows a primarily volume-driven rise in authorized acute hospital spending, with a smaller added unit-cost signal in UTI and cellulitis. The increase is concentrated in metabolic disorder, UTI, hip/femur, and cellulitis stays, and MERCY HEALTH - ST. JOSEPH WARREN HOSPITAL is a notable provider concentration point. This pattern needs both utilization management and a limited reimbursement check on the cases showing higher paid per admit.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A mixed pattern needs different actions by component: admission control for most of the spend and pricing review only where payment per stay is also rising.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Use UM to address OH acute hospital admission growth first, then run a focused reimbursement review on UTI and cellulitis stays showing higher paid per admit in OH and the smaller NY / OH pocket.
evidence_summary: OH metabolic disorder admissions add about $117K with 10 more admissions.
MERCY HEALTH - ST. JOSEPH WARREN HOSPITAL adds about $63K with 7 more admissions despite lower paid per admit.
OH UTI cases add about $71K with 8 more admissions and about $1K higher paid per admit.
NY cellulitis adds about $34K with 3 more admissions and about $2K higher paid per admit.

key_driver_codes: Miscellaneous Disorders of Nutrition, Metabolism, and Fluids and Electrolytes with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: OH clinical growth is concentrated inside one inpatient category: metabolic and electrolyte conditions. Most of the pressure comes from more admissions, with some additional payment intensity in hypernatremia-related stays. This is a focused clinical management opportunity rather than a broad change across inpatient services.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A narrow diagnosis set allows targeted admission criteria, observation use, and care pathway intervention.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Assign clinical and UM teams to review OH admission criteria and care pathways for electrolyte and fluid-balance diagnoses, especially cases that could be treated in lower-intensity settings.
evidence_summary: Hyponatremia adds about $109K with 10 more admissions.
Fluid overload adds about $38K with 6 more admissions.
Hypokalemia adds about $75K with 6 more admissions.
Hyperosmolality and hypernatremia adds about $55K with 5 more admissions and about $2.7K higher paid per admit.

business_patterns.pattern_details: A meaningful share of remaining spend is driven by rare, high-cost inpatient cases across multiple providers rather than recurring volume. Most of these signals come from one to three admissions at a time, often with very high paid per admit and unusual clinical presentations. These cases should be handled through case-level review and payment validation, not broad utilization or network policy changes.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Low-count outliers can materially distort trend results and need a different response than recurring admission growth.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Open case-level reviews for the named providers and DRGs to confirm clinical severity, coding accuracy, and payment integrity, then separate true catastrophic cases from actionable recurring patterns.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Most of the impact comes from one- to three-admission spikes with low baseline counts, so case legitimacy and payment accuracy should be confirmed before broader action.
evidence_summary: MARY WASHINGTON HOSPITAL INC in VA shows multiple single-case spikes, including cardiac valve replacement at about $35K and an unrelated major O.R. procedure at about $35K.
DCH REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER in GA has rare infection and surgical outliers, including candidal sepsis at about $38K and a dialysis catheter complication surgery at about $29K.
MERCY HEALTH - ST. JOSEPH WARREN HOSPITAL in OH and MARY WASHINGTON HOSPITAL INC in VA also show rare sepsis and heart failure outliers ranging from about $14K to $29K per case.
These groups are dominated by one to three admissions each.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Smaller provider and site-specific inpatient spikes are emerging in VA, ME, and MO
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Provider and site-specific authorized inpatient activity at MARY WASHINGTON HOSPITAL INC, CRITICAL ACCESS in ME, and SSM HEALTH DEPAUL HOSPITAL - ST. LOUIS

providers: SSM HEALTH DEPAUL HOSPITAL - ST. LOUIS

key_driver_codes: SSM HEALTH DEPAUL HOSPITAL - ST. LOUIS
business_patterns.pattern_details: Several smaller operational spikes are concentrated in individual providers or sites with low starting volumes. The largest is MARY WASHINGTON HOSPITAL INC in VA, while ME CRITICAL ACCESS and MO Medicare HMO show small but high-cost inpatient episodes. These look more like emerging provider mix changes or isolated site-level events than broad product-wide trends.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Low-baseline provider shifts can grow quickly and are best addressed early with targeted provider and site management.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Have network and UM teams confirm whether these are sustained referral or site-of-care changes; if sustained, set provider-specific action plans, and if isolated, exclude them from broader policy conclusions.
business_patterns.validation_reason: These patterns are flagged as low baseline or low volume, so they need confirmation before being treated as durable trends.
evidence_summary: MARY WASHINGTON HOSPITAL INC in VA adds about $298K from 20 more authorized acute hospital admissions.
ME CRITICAL ACCESS cellulitis cases add about $44K across 2 admissions, with about $21.8K higher paid per admit.
SSM HEALTH DEPAUL HOSPITAL - ST. LOUIS in MO Medicare HMO adds about $20K from 1 additional admission with about $20.3K paid per admit.

executive_summary.headline: The biggest cost story is a mix of GA authorization and mapping issues, recurring authorized acute hospital admission growth, and a smaller set of provider-specific outliers.
executive_summary.primary_business_message: GA should be addressed first because it contains both the largest validation issue and the clearest recurring inpatient cost growth. Outside GA, most operational pressure is volume-led in authorized acute hospital admissions, while the remaining spend is concentrated in low-count, high-cost provider outliers that need case-level review rather than broad policy changes.
recommended_focus_order: Validate GA and PA authorization and facility mapping before taking action.
Address GA authorized acute hospital growth and DCH concentration with joint UM and network review.
Manage recurring PPO Local acute hospital admission growth in CA, CT / MO / NY / PA, and OH, while separating true rare outliers for case-level review.

notes: Patterns were kept focused on authorization, provider concentration, utilization growth, validation, and low-baseline outliers.
GA received multiple patterns because it contains distinct validation, operational, and clinical mechanisms with different downstream actions.
Rare high-cost clinical groups were consolidated into one outlier pattern because they share the same business mechanism and case-level action.
